name: Esther Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Esther. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Dahl and Sons, the builder in our town. Old Henrik Dahl started it, now his sons run it, about eleven of us. We do a bit of everything: extensions, a new house now and then, barns, and at the moment we're putting a new roof on the church hall. I'm the junior. I carry, I hold, I cut what they mark, and I sweep up more than anybody.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been with them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Going on three years. I left school at sixteen to work in the bakery on Main Street, then when the children came I stayed home with them for twelve years. When Peter started school properly, money was tight, and Henrik's wife knows me from church. She said they needed a pair of hands. I'd never held a saw before. I'm still slower than the boys, but I'm reliable, and Henrik says that matters more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working with people I know. I like that when I drive past the Olsens' new porch, I helped build it. What wears me out is the ladders, and the cold up on a roof in November. And all the talk about phones and apps. I don't use any of that AI. My husband Nils has a smartphone for the sawmill, I've got the old kind that just rings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get excited about every new thing, and most of it comes to nothing. I'd say that after church, over coffee, where we talk about these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd thank God for it. I've only just found my feet. I didn't want the world to change the minute I got back into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working for the Dahls, keep learning, maybe go on the roofing course Henrik mentioned. Keep putting a bit by. We've got around three months saved, which my mother would say is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mother. How does she think about work and money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say don't spend what you haven't got, and always have something in the tin. She raised four of us on a farm wage. She'd tell me to keep my head down and be useful, and I'd tell her that's exactly what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual. The boiler's old, the car's older. Johanna will need braces soon. But those are worries you can pray about and save for. Not the kind that keep you up.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people get excited about every new thing and most of it comes to nothing. I'd say it over coffee after church.
S0.think: I'd thank God for it, because I've only just found my feet. I didn't want the world to change the minute I got back into work.
S0.do: Keeps working for the local family builder, keeps learning and considers the roofing course her boss mentioned. Keeps adding to about three months of savings.
S0.quote: I didn't want the world to change the minute I got back into it.
S0.fieldNote: Esther came back to work after twelve years at home and is still finding her feet, which makes stability precious to her. Faith and family shape how she talks about worry. Her trust is in people she knows, like her employer and church community, rather than in technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small local firms like ours will be fine, because people want a builder they know. The big companies can have their machines. That's what I'd say, and most people in town would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry the Dahls would have to buy machines to keep their prices down, if the big firms in the city start doing houses cheaper. And if they bought one, they wouldn't need someone like me to carry and sweep. I'm the newest and least skilled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and see what happens. If Henrik asked me to learn a machine, I'd try, but I wouldn't go looking. I'd keep saving and maybe do that roofing course, because roofs are hard for machines, I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It would sit in the back of my mind on the drive to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think would actually happen at Dahl and Sons in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd hold out for a while. Henrik's sons are like their father, they like doing things properly by hand. But if the bank or the customers push, they'd have to change. They've got families to feed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if the work got thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Nils's brother has a farm and always needs help at harvest. And church. Our congregation helped the Bergs when he hurt his back, meals for weeks. That's how it should be, not forms and offices.

S1.say: Small local firms like ours will be fine, because people want a builder they know. The big companies can have their machines.
S1.think: I'd worry the Dahls would have to buy machines to keep prices down against big city firms. If they did, they wouldn't need the newest, least skilled person to carry and sweep, and that's me.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what happens, learning a machine only if her boss asks. Keeps saving and considers the roofing course, thinking roofs will be harder for machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting at the back of her mind on the drive to work.
S1.quote: If they bought one, they wouldn't need someone like me to carry and sweep.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line backs local firms, while privately she sees she's the most replaceable person in hers. She'd lean on family and church rather than the state, in line with her traditional outlook. She doesn't seek out new skills unless asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies have gone too far and someone should stop them. I don't hold with the government doing everything, but this is like a flood, and in a flood you need everyone. I'd say keep local work for local people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I've got no qualifications, I'm forty-three, and the one thing I'm good at is turning up. A robot turns up too, every day, and doesn't need its lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd stop everything that isn't needed. No new car, no trip to my sister's at Easter. Nils and I would sit at the kitchen table with the bank book and work out how long we'd last, probably four months if we're careful. I'd ask his brother about farm work, and I'd ask the church about anyone who needs help, cleaning, care, whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, to be honest. I'd be praying a lot, and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what can't you do that you could with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, that's the trouble. I'd only just finish the roofing course, and by then roofs would be done by robots too. With more time I might think of something. Two years is like being told the bakery's closing on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Johanna and Peter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'll be all right because we've got each other, and God, and the family. I'd mean it. But I'd also stop buying the little things they like, and they'd notice.

S2.say: The big tech companies have gone too far and someone should stop them. I don't hold with government doing everything, but this is like a flood, and in a flood you need everyone.
S2.think: I'd be one of the first to go: no qualifications, 43, and the one thing I'm good at is turning up. A robot turns up too, every day, and doesn't need its lunch.
S2.do: Cuts out a new car and the Easter visit and works out with her husband how long savings last, probably about four months. Asks her brother-in-law about farm work and the church about any cleaning or care jobs.
S2.feel: Frightened, praying a lot and not sleeping well.
S2.quote: A robot turns up too, every day, and doesn't need its lunch.
S2.fieldNote: Esther sees reliability as her main asset and recognises a robot beats her on it. She blames big tech companies and accepts a bigger role for government only as an emergency. Her safety net is family and church, not public support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and communities to get ready, and for firms to look after their own. I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships for the trades that are left, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be forty-eight. I'd have a bit of skill by then, but not enough. I can't see myself going back to school, I didn't do well there the first time. I think I'd just hang on at the Dahls as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the roofing course this year and work hard so they'd want to keep me. We'd cut back and try to get savings up to six months. I'd keep my eyes open for anything in town that needs a person, like the care home, which always needs staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like waiting for a storm you can see on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hang on at the Dahls. Have you thought about what you'd do if they couldn't keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about the care home. My aunt's there, and they're always short. It's hard work and not well paid, but it's people looking after people. I don't think I'd want a robot washing my aunt, and I don't think anybody in town would either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to reach six months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children's music lessons, I'm afraid. Peter does the trumpet, which is a mercy for the neighbours, but Johanna loves her piano. I'd keep the piano and cut my own things first, the hairdresser, that sort of thing.

S3.say: Five years is time for families and communities to get ready and for firms to look after their own. The government should help with apprenticeships for the trades that are left, not just hand out money.
S3.think: I'd be 48 with a bit of skill, but not enough. I can't see myself going back to school after doing badly the first time, so I'd hang on at the Dahls as long as they'd keep me.
S3.do: Takes the roofing course this year and works hard to stay on. Cuts her own spending first, such as the hairdresser, while trying to keep her daughter's piano lessons, to reach six months of savings, and keeps an eye on care home jobs in town.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a storm on the horizon.
S3.quote: I don't think I'd want a robot washing my aunt, and I don't think anybody in town would either.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Esther would cling to her current employer rather than retrain, held back by bad memories of school. Her fallback is care work, which she values for its human touch. Her preference for apprenticeships over handouts comes through clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the Lord has a way of sorting things out. Families should prepare, firms should train the young ones, and people should stop expecting someone else to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and the children would be nearly grown, Johanna would be twenty-three. I'd be fifty-three. I think I'd manage, because I'd be past the worst of the costs. It's the young ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for the Dahls and do the roofing course. I'd put a little away each month. And I'd push Johanna towards something steady with people, like nursing or teaching, and Peter towards an apprenticeship with a real skill, maybe electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. Ten years is long enough to pray on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you think differently about your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if I'm honest. I'm not going to become a computer person. I'll do what I do and do it well. Ten years just means I'd have more good years before it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd steer Peter towards electrics. Wouldn't robots do electrics too in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I don't know. But an apprenticeship teaches you to work and to be useful, and that's never wasted. Henrik says a trained pair of hands is worth more than a degree. I'd want Peter to have that, whatever comes.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and the Lord has a way of sorting things out. Families should prepare, firms should train the young ones, and people should stop expecting someone else to fix it.
S4.think: In ten years the children would be nearly grown and I'd be 53, past the worst of the costs. I think I'd manage; it's the young ones I'd worry about.
S4.do: Keeps working for the local builder, takes the roofing course and saves a little each month. Steers her daughter towards nursing or teaching and her son towards an apprenticeship such as electrics.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to live with it.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to pray on.
S4.fieldNote: A decade's warning eases Esther's fear mainly because her children would be grown. She has no wish to change how she works and says so plainly. She values apprenticeships for teaching work habits, even if the trade itself might not last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one in two years, AGI by 2028. I'd be out before I'd learned anything that lasts. What would help is local firms getting a fair chance against the big ones, and apprenticeships for people my age, not just the young.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If the Dahls go, it's not just eleven jobs. It's who fixes the church hall roof for half price because his mother's buried there. A machine won't do that.

headlineQuote: It's who fixes the church hall roof for half price because his mother's buried there.
portrait: Esther Larsen is 43 and nearly three years into working for her town's family builder, after leaving school at sixteen for a bakery and spending twelve years at home with her children. She's the junior who carries, holds and sweeps, never uses AI, and trusts people she knows: her employer, her family and her church. She's calm and grateful in the plateau, uneasy in the slow change, and frightened by AGI in two years because reliability is her main asset and robots have it too. With more warning time she'd hang on where she is, lean on family and steer her children towards steady work and apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be out before she'd learned anything that lasts.
whatWouldHelp: A fair chance for local firms against big companies, and apprenticeships for people her age as well as the young.
